chunks: Al-Abbas from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'Do I shade myself while I am in ihram?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'Then do I shade myself and offer expiation?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'And if I get sick?' He said, 'Shade yourself and offer expiation.'

Then he said, 'Did you not know that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: There is no pilgrim who sacrifices while responding (to the call of Hajj) until the sun sets, except that his sins disappear with it.'

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And he should not bleed himself by scraping his skin, nor should he be excessive in his siwak so as to bleed his mouth, nor should he rub his face during his washing in wudu and in other than it, so that hair does not fall from it.

key_terms.إِحْرَامٌ: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.مُلَبِّياً: Responding (to the call of God, i.e., saying Talbiyah)

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for shading oneself and offering expiation while in the state of ihram during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* clarifies the juristic distinction between general shading (prohibited without expiation) and shading due to illness (permitted with expiation), reflecting the Shia emphasis on medical necessity in ritual purity. It further links the physical state of the pilgrim to spiritual purification, citing the Prophet’s promise that sacrifices and *talbiyah* until sunset erase sins, while adding practical details on avoiding excessive grooming that causes bleeding or hair loss.
